candidates.title: Use retrieval, not bigger models, for rare-entity factoid questions
candidates.rule: When an agent must answer factoid questions about entities with little web support, route to a retrieval-augmented prompt rather than relying on a larger closed-book model; scaling parameters buys far less accuracy on long-tail facts than adding retrieved passages.
candidates.passage: Overall, retrieval-augmented models outperform their closed-book counterparts across all ranges of relevant document counts, and especially on rare examples.
candidates.finding: GPT-Neo models augmented with top-3 BM25 Wikipedia paragraphs beat closed-book counterparts on Natural Questions, most notably on low-document-count questions; oracle gold-paragraph prompting removed the long-tail penalty entirely. By contrast, a log-linear BLOOM scaling fit (R^2=0.98) on NQ questions with <100 relevant documents extrapolates to needing >10^18 parameters to match a supervised baseline.
workloads: Natural Questions (few-shot closed-book, oracle-paragraph, and BM25-augmented)
candidates.conditions: 4-shot prompting (2-shot for oracle retrieval); BM25 retriever over Wikipedia with top-3 paragraphs inserted into both in-context examples and test question; exact-match scoring; English only.
candidates.limitations: Single paper; 2021-2022 models predating modern instruction-tuned LLMs. Retrieval corpus is Wikipedia, well matched to NQ, so gains may not transfer to domains without a good corpus. BM25 recall itself still mildly declines with low document count. The scaling extrapolation to 10^18 parameters is an extrapolation far outside measured range, not an observation.
candidates.validation_test: On a held-out set of factoid questions binned by entity rarity, compare closed-book accuracy of a small and a much larger current model against the small model plus top-3 retrieved passages, at matched inference cost; check whether retrieval closes the rare-bin gap more than scaling does.

candidates.title: Do not expect modest pre-training data scaling or source diversification to fix long-tail gaps
candidates.rule: Do not plan to close long-tail factual gaps by adding moderately more or more-diverse web pre-training data; treat added web corpora as largely redundant for rare facts and budget for retrieval or targeted data instead.
candidates.passage: Despite having different collection methodologies, these pre-training datasets are highly correlated in terms of how much information they contain related to different QA pairs.
candidates.finding: The paper measures Spearman rank correlations of 0.87-0.97 between relevant-document counts across ROOTS, Pile, C4, OpenWebText and Wikipedia, and observes log-scaled accuracy gains, but it does not run a controlled data-scaling or data-mixing experiment. The recommendation is an inference from the high cross-corpus redundancy plus the roughly log-linear accuracy-vs-count curves.
workloads: TriviaQA relevant-document counts across five corpora
TriviaQA/Natural Questions accuracy binned by document count
candidates.conditions: English web-scraped corpora of 39GB-825GB collected 2019-2022; factoid QA with entity-linkable answers.
candidates.limitations: No matched data-scaling experiment was run; the claim rests on correlation of corpus statistics and an extrapolated curve. Does not cover deliberately curated or synthetic long-tail data, non-English sources, or repeated-epoch training, which the authors raise only as untested ideas.
candidates.validation_test: Pre-train matched-size models on 1x vs 5x web data from independently collected sources and compare accuracy specifically on questions with <10 relevant documents in the 1x corpus.

reason: The paper tests closed-book vs retrieval-augmented QA accuracy stratified by pre-training relevant-document count, and fits scaling trends. Two actionable rules follow: prefer retrieval over scaling for rare-entity factoid questions, and treat entity co-occurrence counts as a usable prior for when a model's parametric answer is unreliable. Both are scoped to few-shot factoid QA on TriviaQA/NQ with 2021-2022 era models.
